description: Özdemir Bayraktar Havacılık ve Uzay Teknolojileri MTAL'den, havacılık, uzay ve yapay zekâ alanında proje geliştiren bir öğrenci ekibiyiz. TUA Astro Hackathon'da Ankara ikincisi, finalde Türkiye şampiyonu olduk; İstinye DataMedX'te üçüncülük aldık. Hızla ürün çıkarmayı ve baskı altında karar vermeyi öğrendik. Radyasyon kalkanlama, yapay zekâ ve veri analizi tecrübemiz var.
summary:
The project is an interface that turns NASA’s microgravity combustion knowledge into fire safety insights for human space exploration. Users pick a material from a built-in library of 70+ solids, liquids, and gases, set the environment (Earth, ISS, Moon, or Mars), oxygen level, and pressure, and our physics engines return a flammability risk level with a confidence rating.
Every material is labeled: calibrated in the engine, linked to NASA PSI data points, mapped to the closest calibrated reference, or flagged as no data, non-flammable, or oxidizer. An AI chatbot selects which of the four physics engines (pyrolysis, droplet evaporation, gas-phase kinetics, and radiation) applies to each material, explains results in plain language, and generates reports.
At its core, we built four physics engines on OpenFOAM, based on the Saffire, BASS, and FLEX investigations and calibrated with data from 2,800 research papers, to simulate burning fabric, fuel droplets, and gaseous fuels at different gravity levels.
The project makes scattered data easy to find and interpret, and extends it to lunar and Martian gravity, where PSI has no data. Results are model predictions, not certified approvals.
details:
What it does and how it works: The system works in three layers behind a single interface. The data layer organizes NASA PSI combustion investigations and links every material in our library to the measurements that exist for it. The physics layer is our own set of four physics engines (pyrolysis, droplet evaporation, gas-phase kinetics, and radiation), built on OpenFOAM, which compute flame behavior and flammability for solid, liquid, and gaseous fuels at the chosen gravity, oxygen concentration, and pressure. The AI layer, a chatbot powered by a large language model, helps the user choose which physics engines apply, answers questions, and explains results in plain language. The output is a flammability risk level with a confidence rating and an exportable report.

The interface gives access to four calibrated reference physics engines. When a user selects a material, the AI assistant compares its type, geometry, and combustion properties with the available engines and recommends the most suitable one. The selected engine is shown on the material card, and materials without a direct match are clearly labeled as mapped to the closest reference.

The physics foundation is OpenFOAM 14. Standard OpenFOAM does not include all the fire physics we need, so we wrote two engines ourselves as custom C++ libraries and built the other two by calibrating OpenFOAM’s own models:

Pyrolysis engine (custom C++). A two-component solid pyrolysis model with fitted rate parameters and fractional reaction orders, calibrated against Saffire-III data and coupled to the gas phase through the multi-region solver foamMultiRun.

Droplet evaporation engine (custom C++). Evaporation and ignition models for droplet clouds, used for liquid fuels such as n-heptane.

Gas-phase kinetics engine (calibrated OpenFOAM reaction model). An adapted two-step methane combustion scheme with calibrated rate constants (T in K):

Radiation engine (calibrated OpenFOAM radiation model). A discrete-ordinates radiation model, calibrated for our cases, that carries heat between the flame, the fuel, and the surroundings.

Both the models and the physics engines were calibrated and trained using data from 2,800 research papers.

The cases are based on the Saffire, BASS, and FLEX investigations: a Saffire-III-style fabric flame spread case, n-heptane droplet combustion as studied in FLEX, and a methane leak in a spacecraft cabin as a gaseous-fuel case. The fabric case is a two-dimensional, symmetric half-domain model. The cases are run at microgravity, lunar (1.62 m/s²), and Martian (3.71 m/s²) gravity, and the droplet and gas cases are also run at Earth gravity for comparison. The methane-leak simulation is a demonstration and has not yet been validated against experimental data. Each library material is linked to NASA PSI data points where they exist; materials without data are mapped to the closest calibrated reference fuel and clearly labeled.

Simulation results: Gravity visibly changes flame behavior. In the methane-leak case, the flame is a compact ellipsoid in microgravity and becomes an elongated, buoyancy-driven plume as gravity increases through lunar, Martian, and Earth values. In the n-heptane droplet case, a hot flame (maximum temperature about 2,800 K) is present at 1 s in microgravity and at lunar gravity, whereas at Martian and Earth gravity the flame has weakened or gone out. In the fabric case, flame spread under 0.245 m/s forced flow shows little sensitivity to gravity. These are preliminary results for single configurations and are presented as predictions.

Benefits and intended impact: PSI data is hard to find, compare, and interpret, and it contains no partial-gravity results. The project gives researchers, engineers, and students one place to explore that data and to estimate fire behavior at lunar and Martian gravity. This supports material selection and early-stage fire safety assessment for Moon bases and pressurized rovers, and the same approach can inform fire safety on Earth.

Tools and technologies: OpenFOAM 14 on Linux, with two custom C++ physics engines (pyrolysis and droplet evaporation) and two calibrated OpenFOAM models (gas-phase kinetics and radiation), run with the multi-region solver foamMultiRun; Python scripts for mesh generation; an interface hosted on Netlify; GitHub for version control; and a large language model (LLM) for the chatbot, engine selection, and result interpretation.

Creativity: Most scientific data tools stop at searching and plotting. This project combines curated NASA PSI data, four physics engines built on OpenFOAM, and an AI chatbot in a single workflow, so a user can go from “which material?” to “how risky is it on the Moon?” in a few clicks. Its most distinctive idea is treating uncertainty as a feature: every material carries a visible status (“calibrated”, “PSI data points available”, “no data”), so users always see what is measured and what is extrapolated.

Factors considered:

Scope: PSI does not cover rocket propellant combustion, so the project focuses on fire safety in habitable environments such as spacecraft, Moon and Mars bases, and pressurized rovers.

Partial-gravity gap: PSI has no partial-gravity data, so lunar and Martian behavior is estimated by simulation and presented as prediction.

Exploration atmospheres: Flammability depends strongly on oxygen concentration and pressure, and planned Moon habitats are expected to use 30% oxygen or more, so these inputs are adjustable rather than fixed to Earth air.

Uncertainty: Materials without data are mapped to the closest calibrated reference fuel and labeled, and results are model predictions that do not replace official material certification.
